steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Analysing dance performance involves watching closely and breaking down what you observe into component parts

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Live performance offers a full sensory experience — you feel the energy, scale and atmosphere of the work

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Recorded performance allows repeated viewing, enabling closer analysis of specific moments and details

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: A structured approach uses the four content categories: action, dynamics, space and relationships

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is the advantage of watching a live performance over a recorded one? | Q: Why is repeated viewing useful when analysing a recorded dance? | Q: How do the four content categories help structure an analysis?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Live performance provides the full sensory experience — you feel the energy, scale and atmosphere in real time, and the audience-performer relationship is immediate and tangible. | Repeated viewing lets you focus on different elements each time — first the overall structure, then specific movement details, design features or dancer relationships. | They provide a systematic framework so you cover all aspects: action (what), dynamics (how), space (where) and relationships (who), ensuring nothing is missed.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When analysing a recorded work, watch it at least twice — once for overall impression, once for specific detail Structure your analysis using the four content categories to ensure a thorough response Always link what you observe to the choreographic intention — explain how features serve the purpose Include design elements in your analysis when relevant — costume, lighting and sound contribute to meaning In exam answers, use specific examples from the work rather than vague generalisations
